The Great Plague of London. In 1665 and 1666, a major outbreak of bubonic plague killed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 people in London—roughly 15 to 20 percent of the city's population. It was the last major plague pandemic to strike England and occurred just before the Great Fire of London, which many believed had cleansed the city of the disease.

The plague struck during the reign of King Charles II, when much of the court and nobility had fled the city. It spread primarily through flea-infested rats in crowded tenements and trade districts. Mortality was highest among the poor who could not flee or isolate. The peak death toll in September 1665 exceeded 7,000 per week according to the bills of mortality kept by parish clerks, though these figures likely undercount the true deaths.

The city responded with drastic quarantine measures. Houses of infected persons were marked with a red cross and sealed shut. Entire families were locked inside while guards were stationed outside. The social breakdown was severe. Contemporary accounts describe the stench of mass burial pits and the courage and desperation of those who remained.

The most vivid eyewitness accounts come from Samuel Pepys, whose famous diary documents the plague's social impact and the psychological trauma of the crisis. The Great Fire of London in September 1666 is sometimes credited with ending the plague by destroying rat habitats, though the disease had already begun declining by that point.
